newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Hekmatyar stays aloof from anti-Taleban alliance.
newsitem.headline: Hekmatyar stays aloof from anti-Taleban alliance.

text.p: Ousted Afghan Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar opposes the radical Islamic Taleban now ruling Kabul, but does not want President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government to return to power, a spokesman said on Wednesday.

"We are not striving to reinstall the previous regime," Ghairat Baheer, designated ambassador to Islamabad by Rabbani, told Reuters in the Pakistani capital. "Our efforts are geared to the establishment of a government of all sides."

His remarks were the clearest sign yet that Hekmatyar has fallen out with his erstwhile colleagues in the Rabbani government, while remaining hostile to the Taleban, potent rivals for the loyalty of Afghanistan's ethnic Pashtun tribes.
Baheer, a senior member of Hekmatyar's mainly Pashtun Hezb-i-Islami party, said the party wanted a "clean" interim government to be installed in Kabul to prepare for elections.
He said Hekmatyar had not taken part in talks in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif and elsewhere aimed at forging a military alliance of anti-Taleban factions.

Ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, Uzbek militia commander General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction leader Karim Khalili signed a mutual defence pact against the Taleban in the north last week.
"We will only particpate in a front that can represent the whole nation and is based on social realities," Baheer said.
Hekmatyar fled to northern Afghanistan with the rest of the Rabbani government after the Taleban swept into Kabul on September 27. Baheer said he was now in Baglan province.
Once a bitter foe of Masood, he rejoined the Rabbani administration in June under a peace deal that ended a 2-1/2-year revolt he had staged in alliance with Dostum.
Hezb-i-Islami received the lion's share of guns and money funnelled from Western and Arab sponsors of Afghan guerrilla groups by Pakistan during the anti-Soviet struggle in the 1980s.
But the Taleban's advance over the past two years into most areas once held by Hekmatyar, has severely weakened him.

Baheer said Hezb-i-Islami forces in the provinces of Kapisa and Parwan near Kabul had been ordered to defend their territory and not allow the "bitter experiences of occupation" to be repeated. He did not identify Hezb-i-Islami's enemies.
Baheer said Hezb-i-Islami opposed all forms of foreign intervention and denied that the ousted government had received any military or financial assistance from anywhere.
"If a particular group has received help, it should not be considered as assistance to the government," he added.
